1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. SLO: service level objective; RACI: responsible, accountable, consulted, informed; ADR: architecture decision record; DPIA: data protection impact assessment; LLM: large language model; SLI: service level indicator

  • Structured discovery: questions, stakeholders, requirements
  • How to communicate architecture decisions and trade-offs to different audiences
  • Expectation management: honest limits, SLAs, SLOs
  • Feedback loops with stakeholders

2Structured Discovery

Running case

Lumen Advisory Runs Discovery for an Airline's Disruption Assistant

  • The airline wants an assistant to rebook passengers during disruptions
  • Operations, legal, customer care, IT security and the CFO each want different things

Area Questions Output
Business value What outcome, for whom, worth what? What happens if we do nothing? Goals, pillars, targets (Module 1)
Process and users How is the work done today? Who touches it? Where are the pain points and volumes? Process map, personas, baselines
Data What data exists, where, how clean, who owns it, how sensitive? Data inventory, access rules
Systems Which systems to integrate; APIs, auth, limits? Integration list, constraints
Risk and compliance Which regulations, policies, audit needs; what failures are unacceptable? Risk register, regimes (Module 14)
Quality How will we know it works? Examples of good and bad outputs? Eval dataset seeds, acceptance criteria
Non-functional Latency, availability, scale, cost ceiling Target SLOs, budget
Operations Who runs it, supports it, owns prompts and knowledge? RACI, runbook outline

Practices

  • Interview every stakeholder group, not only the sponsor; ask for real examples (tickets, documents, edge cases).
  • Separate needs from solutions: "faster rebooking", not "an agent".
  • Prioritize requirements (must, should, could) and record assumptions and open questions with owners.
  • Run a thin prototype early to turn opinions into evidence.
  • Capture constraints that shape the architecture: data residency, platform standards, skills, timelines.
Exam tip

Good discovery gathers measurable outcomes, real examples, data and risk constraints from all stakeholder groups before any design commitment.

3Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs

Audience Needs Format
Executives Outcome, cost, risk, timeline, decision needed One-page summary, options with a recommendation
Engineers Components, interfaces, patterns, test strategy Architecture diagrams, ADRs, API specs
Security, legal, compliance Data flows, controls, retention, residency Data-flow diagram, control mapping, DPIA inputs
Operators and support How to run, monitor, escalate Runbooks, dashboards, limits
End users What it does, what it does not, how to get help Plain-language guidance, disclosure

Presenting a decision

  1. State the decision and the problem it solves.
  2. Show options (at least two or three) with criteria (cost, latency, accuracy, risk, effort).
  3. Give a recommendation and the trade-offs accepted.
  4. List assumptions, risks and mitigations, and what would change the decision.
  5. Record it as an architecture decision record (ADR) [Beyond the guide].
  • Quantify trade-offs with evaluation results and measured cost and latency, not adjectives.
  • Be honest about limits: Claude can be wrong, outputs need validation, knowledge has a cutoff, quality is probabilistic, behavior can change with model versions.
  • Do not promise perfect accuracy, zero risk or fixed outcomes; give ranges and confidence.

4SLAs, SLOs and Expectation Alignment

Term Meaning LLM-specific notes
SLA Commitment to a customer, often contractual Promise only what the system and dependencies can deliver
SLO Internal target that supports the SLA Set for latency (p95), availability, quality (eval score), cost
SLI The measured indicator Time to first token, error rate, faithfulness rate, escalation rate
Error budget Allowed shortfall Governs release pace
  • An SLA for an LLM system depends on platform availability, rate limits, capacity and model behavior; plan retries with backoff, fallbacks (another model or platform, cached answers, human handoff) and capacity (rate-limit tiers, batch for non-urgent work).
  • Separate performance SLAs (speed, uptime) from quality targets (accuracy), because quality is statistical: specify it as percent on a defined test set and sampled production, not "always correct".
  • Human review time counts toward end-to-end SLAs.
  • Align expectations early: demos use curated inputs; share the eval set and failure examples.

5Feedback Loops

  • Channels: in-product thumbs and comments, reviewer overrides, support tickets, steering reviews, metric dashboards.
  • Regular cadence: a review forum with sponsors, operators and risk.
  • Triage feedback into categories (prompt, retrieval, data, tool, UX, policy) and prioritize by impact.
  • Close the loop: tell stakeholders what changed and why; add feedback cases to the eval set.
  • Manage scope: new requests get impact analysis (cost, risk, latency) before acceptance.
Exam tip

Run discovery with all stakeholder groups, ask for real examples, and separate needs from solutions.

Exam tip

Quality is statistical: write SLAs as measurable targets on a test set, never as "always correct".

6Exam Q&A

S1A sponsor says "just build an agent." What is the best discovery response?

  • AAsk the sponsor to write the system prompt so that the requirements are captured in the sponsor's own words
  • BAsk for outcomes, baselines, real examples, constraints and stakeholders before choosing a pattern
  • CStart building an agent so that the sponsor sees visible progress and the team learns from the first demo
  • DChoose the largest model and demonstrate
Show the answer

Answer: B. Discovery separates needs from solutions and produces testable requirements.

S2Which stakeholder group is most likely to be missed in early discovery and cause late surprises?

  • AThe marketing team
  • BThe team that will write the first demo
  • CRisk, compliance and security owners
  • DThe people who will use the tool in their daily workflow only
Show the answer

Answer: C. Late discovery of regulatory or security constraints forces redesign.

S3An executive asks for a recommendation among three architectures. How should the architect present it?

  • AAsk the executive to choose without a recommendation
  • BPresent a deep technical comparison of embeddings and chunk sizes
  • CPresent only the preferred option with its advantages
  • DState the options against agreed criteria, recommend one with accepted trade-offs, and list assumptions and risks
Show the answer

Answer: D. Executives need options, a recommendation, risks and a decision.

S4A client demands "100 percent accuracy" in an SLA for an LLM assistant. What should the architect do?

  • APromise it only for the first month
  • BExplain that quality is statistical, and agree measurable targets on a defined test set and sampled production, with human review for critical cases
  • CAccept it to win the contract and rely on prompt improvements
  • DRemove accuracy from the SLA entirely
Show the answer

Answer: B. Set honest, measurable quality targets rather than absolute promises.

S5Which TWO are valid components of a performance SLO for an interactive assistant? Select TWO.

  • AAvailability or error rate within an agreed budget
  • BThe exact wording of every answer
  • Cp95 latency and time to first token under defined thresholds
  • DA promise that the model never changes
  • EGuaranteed zero hallucinations
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. Performance objectives are measurable operational indicators such as p95 latency and error rate, not promises about every answer.

S6What should be included when documenting a major design decision?

  • AOnly the final choice
  • BA list of the people who disagreed with the decision and the objections that each of them raised
  • CThe vendor's marketing description
  • DContext, options considered, the decision, trade-offs accepted and what would change it
Show the answer

Answer: D. An architecture decision record captures the context, options, decision and trade-offs so future teams understand the reasoning.

S7Which design supports an availability SLA when the model platform is occasionally rate-limited?

  • AA single call with no retry
  • BRetries with exponential backoff, capacity planning, and fallbacks such as another model, cached answers or human handoff
  • CDisabling monitoring to reduce load
  • DRaising max_tokens
Show the answer

Answer: B. Resilience patterns protect the SLA against dependency limits.

S8Stakeholder feedback arrives in tickets, comments and reviewer overrides. What should the team do with it?

  • ATriage it by category and impact, add cases to the eval set, release changes and communicate them
  • BIgnore feedback that cannot be reproduced, since it cannot be tested and is therefore not actionable for the engineering team
  • CUse it only to rewrite the demo
  • DKeep it in a spreadsheet until the quarterly review, then decide which items are worth discussing with sponsors
Show the answer

Answer: A. A closed loop turns feedback into improvements and trust.

S9A demo with curated inputs impressed the sponsor, who now expects the same quality on all production traffic. What should the architect do?

  • AShare the evaluation results and failure examples to reset expectations with evidence
  • BSay nothing so that confidence stays high
  • CLimit production traffic to curated inputs
  • DIncrease the model size without telling the sponsor, so that production quality moves closer to the demo
Show the answer

Answer: A. Sharing evaluation results and failure examples resets expectations with evidence about real performance instead of a curated demo.

S10A new feature request arrives mid-project. What is the best response?

  • AReject all changes
  • BRun an impact analysis on cost, risk, latency and schedule, then prioritize with stakeholders
  • CAssign it to the least busy engineer without analysis, since small requests rarely affect the schedule
  • DAccept it immediately
Show the answer

Answer: B. An impact analysis on cost, risk, latency and schedule lets stakeholders prioritize the request without breaking commitments.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Discovery Business value · process · data · systems · risk · quality · non-functional · operations
Method All stakeholder groups; real examples; needs not solutions; assumptions logged; thin prototype
Message Tailor to audience; options, recommendation, trade-offs, assumptions, ADR
Honesty Probabilistic quality; limits; no absolute promises
SLA / SLO / SLI Commitment / target / measurement; p95 latency, availability, quality on test set
